questions.prompt: What conversion occurs during pyruvate oxidation?

questions.answer_text: Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor; it accepts electrons and protons, forms water, and allows aerobic electron flow to continue.
questions.explanation: Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor. It accepts electrons and protons to form water, and this final acceptance allows aerobic electron flow to continue; without it, flow cannot continue normally. The other choices each change one of these required facts.

options.text: Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor; it accepts electrons and protons, forms water, and allows aerobic electron flow to continue.
Oxygen is not the terminal electron acceptor; it accepts electrons and protons, forms water, and allows aerobic electron flow to continue.
Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor; it accepts only electrons, forms water, and allows aerobic electron flow to continue.
Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor; it accepts electrons and protons, does not form water, and allows aerobic electron flow to continue.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes oxygen's complete role at the end of aerobic electron transport?

questions.answer_text: Fermentation keeps glycolysis running by regenerating NAD+; it uses no oxygen as terminal electron acceptor and produces much less ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration.
questions.explanation: Fermentation does not replace glycolysis; it keeps glycolysis running by regenerating NAD+. It uses no oxygen as a terminal electron acceptor and produces much less ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration. The other choices incorrectly change one of these points.

options.text: Fermentation replaces glycolysis while regenerating NAD+; it uses no oxygen as terminal electron acceptor and produces much less ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration.
Fermentation keeps glycolysis running by regenerating NAD+; it uses no oxygen as terminal electron acceptor and produces much less ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration.
Fermentation keeps glycolysis running but does not regenerate NAD+; it uses no oxygen as terminal electron acceptor and produces much less ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration.
